scenario.title: The 30-Year Acupuncture Clinic's Crossroads
scenario.setting: Tucked between a laundromat and a vintage record shop in a sun-faded Portland industrial neighborhood, the 30-year-old community acupuncture clinic hums with soft guzheng music and the faint scent of mugwort. The waiting room’s frayed knit blankets, chipped ceramic herbal tea mugs, and corkboard crammed with 20 years of handwritten patient thank-you notes feel like a warm, familiar hug. Just last week, the clinic’s founding owner Clara received a formal notice that their landlord is doubling the rent in 60 days, a hike that would make the space unaffordable without either raising prices beyond reach for their low-income regulars or shutting down entirely.

characters.name: Clara Maeve
characters.tendencies: She’s the clinic’s founding owner, who built the sliding-scale community hub after seeing local residents locked out of traditional healthcare, and now faces the impossible choice between saving her business and keeping care affordable for her neighbors.

characters.name: Javi Marquez
characters.tendencies: He’s a volunteer acupuncturist and neighborhood activist who organizes block fundraisers, and urges Clara to launch a viral crowdfunding campaign and protest the landlord’s rent hike.

characters.name: Marcus Hale
characters.tendencies: He’s a pro bono local small business consultant who warns against risky crowdfunding campaigns, and pushes Clara to apply for city grants that come with strict long-term reporting rules.

characters.name: Lila Bennett
characters.tendencies: She’s a long-time low-income patient with chronic back pain who relies on the clinic’s sliding scale, and brings homemade oatmeal raisin cookies to the clinic’s weekly volunteer potlucks to show her gratitude.

turns.name: Clara Maeve
turns.text: "I heard you skipped your blood pressure meds last month because you had to cover your kid’s school supplies. Don’t make that choice again—this care is yours, no strings attached." turns.text:
Clara, we can’t just let the landlord hike your rent out of nowhere—this block’s small tenants need to stick together. I already gathered a crew of neighbors for a protest outside his office Saturday, and I set up a crowdfunding page to cover any emergency moving costs you might incur.

turns.text:
"I know that flashy crowdfunding campaign you were eyeing might look like a quick fix, but it’ll saddle you with tons of unplanned deliverables and backer complaints down the line. The city’s small business manufacturing grant has strict quarterly reporting rules, but it also includes free mentorship and funding tailored to local Portland industrial startups like yours."
[taps a crumpled crowdfunding risk checklist against his knuckles before setting it atop a stack of grant application packets on the scuffed folding table between us]

turns.name: Lila Bennett
turns.text:
These oatmeal raisin cookies are chewier than usual— I had to pause mixing the dough twice when my back seized up overnight. I wanted to thank you all again for working with me on the sliding scale last month when I couldn’t cover my full treatment cost.
[Places a dented floral tin of cookies on the clinic’s front counter, rubbing the small of her sore lower back with one hand while she tilts her head in a warm, tired smile.]

turns.name: Clara Maeve
turns.text:
"Oh Lila, these oatmeal raisin cookies are wonderful, but please don’t push through your back pain to bake them for me—this clinic only works because we look out for each other, not just the patients." turns.name: Javi Marquez
turns.text:
Thanks so much for these perfect cookies, Lila—they’re exactly the pick-me-up this small huddle needs right now. I checked in with a local grassroots organizer this morning who’ll help us craft a streamlined crowdfunding campaign so we don’t get saddled with all the unplanned deliverables Marcus flagged.
[Pulling a stack of bright pink tenant union sign-up sheets from his canvas acupuncture tote and passing them around the group clustered by the record shop’s sidewalk awning]

turns.name: Marcus Hale
turns.text: "I get that crowdfunding seems like a fast way to cover Clara’s rent hike right now, but those campaigns load you down with unplanned deliverables and prying donor demands that’ll only add stress long-term. [taps the crumpled grant packet peeking out of his frayed canvas tote before grabbing one of Lila’s oatmeal raisin cookies]

These have a little extra cinnamon, too, since I figured you all put in so much work for folks like me. I had to sit down on my kitchen floor halfway through mixing because my back locked up bad, but I didn’t want to skip bringing these this week. I hope they taste good enough to make up for the messy, partially paused dough I almost wasted.

scenario.title: The Chime Dilemma of Willowbrook
scenario.setting: The tree-lined square of Willowbrook is anchored by an 118-year-old cast-iron clock tower, its face smudged with decades of rain grime and its hourly chime a familiar, warm tone that had rung over the town since 1905. Retired horologist Elias Voss has cared for the tower for 22 years, performing gentle, historically accurate maintenance every Wednesday afternoon. Last Tuesday, a rusted iron gear snapped mid-strike, silencing the chime entirely and splitting the tight-knit community over how to repair it.

characters.tendencies: Fights to preserve the tower’s original 1903 internal components, refusing to replace vintage parts with modern, cheaper alternatives

characters.name: Mara Hines
characters.tendencies: Pushes for a quick, budget-friendly repair using off-the-shelf parts to get the chime working before the town’s annual harvest festival

characters.name: Javi Marquez
characters.tendencies: Organizes community rallies to demand the tower’s original chime be restored, framing the sound as the town’s collective heartbeat

characters.name: Lila Torres
characters.tendencies: Documents the tower’s history for her local history fair project, caught between respecting Elias’s expertise and Mara’s practical timeline

turns.text:

[brushing a fine layer of tree pollen and rust from the clock’s lower metal face, his calloused fingers lingering a moment on the cool, weathered iron]

turns.name: Mara Hines
turns.text:
Hurry, grab that universal door chime transformer from the corner hardware store—its voltage matches the old clock’s leftover wiring perfectly. We can rig it up in ten minutes to get the chime blaring before the harvest festival crowds arrive, no fancy custom cast-iron parts required.
[Slips a flathead screwdriver into the rusted access panel of the clock tower’s base and pries it open with a sharp twist]

turns.text:
Friends, this 118-year-old clock tower wasn’t just built to tell time—it was designed to ring with the heartbeat of our whole Willowbrook. We can’t let the town council swap that rich, familiar, hand-tuned chime for that tinny, generic electronic tone they’ve been testing this past week. Let’s stand together and demand they give back the sound that ties every one of us here.
[Steps up onto a weathered wooden crate in the square’s center, hoisting a crumpled stack of handwritten petitions above his head to rally the growing crowd]

turns.text:
I’ve been cross-referencing Elias’s handwritten construction logs with the town’s 1905 council minutes for the clock tower exhibit, but Mara says we have to break down the square display in 45 minutes. [adjusts a crumpled black-and-white photo of the 118-year-old tower taped to a display board, fidgeting with a loose poster tack]

That matching universal transformer is still a cheap, modern substitute—nothing can replace the hand-forged 1903 internals that’ve kept this tower running for 118 years. You’re not just rewiring a clock; you’re stripping away the very history that binds this town together.
[He holds up a dented, original cast-iron gear bolt from his tool pouch, turning it in the sunlight to show its worn, hand-polished edges.]

[Snags her scuffed canvas tool roll off the nearby oak bench and dashes toward the downtown hardware shop]

turns.name: Javi Marquez
turns.text:
We can’t let that heartbeat fade away for good. This tower’s 1903 chime hasn’t just marked time—it’s been the quiet backdrop to our wedding exits, our kids’ first soccer game wins, every lazy Sunday evening we’ve spent lounging in this square. Let’s stand together right now and collect signatures for our petition to save the original sound of Willowbrook.
[Kneels to grab a stack of bright pink petition sheets from the base of the nearby oak tree, holding one aloft to catch the afternoon sunlight.]

turns.name: Lila Torres
turns.text:
I get that preserving the tower’s original 1903 internals matters so much, Elias, but we only have 90 minutes until the local history fair setup begins. We can photograph the existing cast-iron parts for the exhibit display instead of rushing to swap out the transformers last minute.
[tapping her crumpled council minute printout against her hip before gesturing toward the tower’s fenced-off lower viewing platform to encourage both of you to collaborate on documenting the original hardware]

The society has just 21 days to raise $7,500 to repair the broken dome winch and replace its cracked 12-inch primary mirror, or the county will foreclose and auction the property to a luxury cabin developer. A fledgling GoFundMe campaign has only hit 12% of its fundraising goal so far, with little momentum beyond a small group of dedicated hobbyist members.

scenario.title: Fading Dials, Hybrid Signals
scenario.setting: KWTL-92.3 Community Radio occupies a converted 1980s fire station annex in the western Appalachian foothills. It operates as a network of volunteer cells: on-air rotation, engineering maintenance, fundraising outreach, and community booking. Sustained by a small core crew of 8 active volunteers, the station has operated past its first full decade of service. Over the past decade, its terrestrial listenership has dropped by exactly half, as locals now prioritize online streaming and social media instead of tuning into terrestrial dials.

characters.name: Marisol Cruz
characters.tendencies: She is the station's lead manager, overseeing all volunteer cells and coordinating grant applications and emergency broadcast schedules. She has spent the past three years leading grant-writing and organizing pledge drives to reverse the station's declining listenership.

characters.name: Lila Mae Jenkins
characters.tendencies: She hosts the weekly Local Folk Hour, inviting local farmers, poets, and retirees to share their work and stories. She has noticed her core regular listeners are mostly over 65, and struggles to recruit younger volunteers or listeners for her show or the station overall.

characters.name: Jai Reddy
characters.tendencies: He is the station's volunteer data auditor, compiling monthly listenership metrics and quarterly reports for the crew. He tracks both terrestrial radio and online stream numbers, identifying gaps in the station's outreach and audience engagement.

characters.name: Eddie "Tink" Marlow
characters.tendencies: He is a retired ham radio operator and volunteer engineering cell member, tinkering with the station's aging broadcast tower and transmitter hardware. He has recently developed a hybrid terrestrial-online broadcast setup that has started drawing a small new cohort of young listeners.

scenario.title: The Fading Lantern Lodge Membership Crisis
scenario.setting: Tucked between a laundromat and a shuttered hardware store in Maplewood’s blue-collar downtown, the Fading Lantern Lodge once drew dozens of locals for weekly bingo nights and pancake breakfasts. Now its front porch only holds a single dented folding chair most days, its windows smudged with grime, and the latest membership drive netted just two new signees in three months. The only regular visitors are a handful of octogenarian members and the occasional teenager stealing shade from the summer sun.

turns.name: Marnie "Mac" MacKenzie
turns.text:
I will not approve any unvoted community outreach initiatives. Our lodge’s operating budget is strictly allocated to hall repairs and annual charter renewal fees, not these frivolous, unsanctioned casual gatherings. Our current membership retention rate sits at just 41%, so every dollar must be accounted for per formal bylaws.
[Tapping a printed membership roster against her clipboard with sharp, deliberate taps as she brushes past a crumpled neighborhood potluck flyer stuck to the lodge’s dented screen door.]

turns.name: Jazmine "Jax" Marlow
turns.text:
Heard my grandpa’s secret blueberry pancake recipe’s headlining this Saturday’s breakfast spread at the lodge—you remember the buttery, syrupy batches we’d sneak extra blueberries for behind his old diner counter back in ‘98? C’mon on down, even if you just need a warm spot out of the crisp downtown wind and a chance to swap old stories.
[Waves a slightly coffee-stained, dog-eared flyer for the pancake breakfast over her head, grinning so wide her dimples poke through her rounded cheeks.]

turns.name: Burt Haggerty
turns.text:
Look, I just swung by for the cheap coffee—didn’t mean to start a fuss, but it’s been three months since I asked about adding a weekly carpentry workshop for folks who don’t want to knit or play bingo. Not a single thing’s changed around here, and I’m not renewing my membership until you guys quit sticking to the same old tired events.
[He shoves a crumpled one-dollar bill across the scuffed Formica counter, grabs his dented stainless steel travel mug full of lukewarm coffee, and trundles toward the exit without a backward glance.]

turns.name: Gloria Hale
turns.text:
Hey neighbor, we’re finally getting our old bingo night back up and running this Saturday afternoon! It’s free to join, we’ve got homemade apple cider and peanut brittle for everyone, and the grand prize is a jar of my mom’s preserved blackberry jam. We’re also collecting gently used winter hats and gloves for the local elementary school’s cozy closet while you’re here.
[Straightening a stack of neon bingo cards on the lodge’s scuffed wooden front counter and tapping a hand-drawn “Bingo This Saturday!” sign into place beside the warped screen door.]

turns.name: Marnie "Mac" MacKenzie
turns.text:
I won’t entertain these unsanctioned, last-minute community offerings—they siphon away our limited operating funds that are meant strictly for hall repairs and charter compliance. Burt, your carpentry works request requires a full membership vote per our official bylaws, not a casual drop-in pitch, and Jax and Gloria’s event plans need to go through the proper approval channels first. I’m not diverting any budget dollars to subsidize pancake spreads or bingo nights right now.
[Taps a dog-eared copy of the lodge’s official bylaws against her clipboard, jaw set tightly]

turns.name: Jazmine "Jax" Marlow
turns.text:
C’mon, Mac—Burt’s been bugging me nonstop about his carpentry spot for three months, and my grandpa’s blueberry pancakes are the perfect way to drag every last neighbor through the lodge doors. We can slot a quick test run of his drop-in hour right after the breakfast line wraps, and Gloria’s already lined up homemade apple cider for bingo anyway, so folks will stick around for hours after that.
[leans in with a soft, playful grin and flutters a crumpled stack of handwritten pancake breakfast sign-up sheets from her worn flannel hip pocket]

turns.name: Burt Haggerty
turns.text:
I saw the bingo notice taped to the laundromat’s bulletin board, and that’s nice for the regulars, but I didn’t trek over here just for a free apple cider. That carpentry workshop I asked about three months back hasn’t gotten so much as a quick reply from the lodge board. I just wanted to offer a low-key space for folks who like fixing things, whether that’s their own porch railings or neighborhood park birdhouses.
[He sets his half-empty, chipped ceramic coffee mug down with a soft clink on the scuffed front counter, crossing his arms over his worn flannel shirt.]

turns.name: Gloria Hale
turns.text:
I also put together a donated prize basket stuffed with local wildflower honey and hand-knit scarves for the bingo night’s top winner, and we’ve got free neon bingo daubers for anyone who forgets their own. It’ll feel just like the cozy, familiar bingo nights we all loved back when the lodge was humming with weekly gatherings.
[I tap a stack of brightly colored bingo cards against the scuffed front wooden counter and nod toward the steaming crockpot of spiced apple cider sitting on a folding table by the door.]

turns.name: Jessa Mae Carver
turns.text:
The developer’s offer is tempting enough to wipe out the back taxes piling up for the past two years. But every time I walk past the chipped concession stand counter, I hear my dad calling out “extra butter for the kids in the blue pickup” like it was yesterday. I can’t just walk away from this place.
[She presses a crumpled polaroid of her teenage self standing beside her dad at the drive-in’s projector booth into her jeans pocket, jaw set softly.]

turns.name: Marnie Cole
turns.text:
Hey there, Willow Creek neighbours! That beloved old drive-in’s got just one last weekend left to stay open before the late summer corn blocks the main screen, and we’ve only scraped together half the cash we need to patch the faulty projector! Every spare dollar, every hour of your time can keep this spot alive—we can’t let our town’s favorite summer hangout turn into a weedy field!
[She waves a stack of neon orange fundraiser flyers above her head, thumping a scuffed work boot against a tumbleweed tangled around the drive-in’s rickety entry sign.]

turns.name: Arthur Hale
turns.text:
I swung by to touch base about your drive-in’s pending loan renewal. The late-summer crop dips haven’t done any favors for your weekend ticket sales, and I know business has been tighter than usual this year, but the regional bank’s strict lending rules are non-negotiable right now. I wish I could push back the repayment deadline, but I can’t overstep my formal authority without board approval.
[taps a crumpled stack of ticket stubs taped to the inside of his leather bank folder before sliding a printed repayment timeline across the hood of his dented pickup truck]

turns.name: Clay Thornton
turns.text:
Back when I ran this very booth, we’d have lines stretched all the way down the cornfield road on nights just like this, when the summer sun lingered just long enough to paint the sky pink. Kids would dart between parked cars with glow sticks, and I’d have to yell over the radio to quiet ’em down before the previews started.
[Wiping a smudge of film emulsion off his worn flannel sleeve before prodding the rusted film reel perched on the projector’s arm]

turns.name: Jessa Mae Carver
turns.text:
I’ve been staring at the chipped concession counter all week, torn between wiping out these back taxes and honoring every memory Dad built here. Clay, you remember how Dad would beam when lines stretched out to the cornfield like that? I can’t just shut this place down without at least trying to hang on.
[She runs a shaky hand along the scuffed wooden edge of the concession counter, not meeting anyone’s eyes for a long beat before lifting her gaze.]

turns.name: Marnie Cole
turns.text:
Clay just reminded us all how this drive-in used to pack the cornfield road back in his booth-running days, and we ain’t letting that legacy fade away now! Between the lagging ticket sales, looming back taxes, and that developer’s tempting offer, one last weekend of packed parking spots is all we need to keep the gates open for good!
[Pounding a fist against the chipped concession counter to drive her point home, already waving a stack of handwritten donation tickets toward the group loitering by the popcorn machine.]

turns.name: Arthur Hale
turns.text:
I know this final weekend is your last shot to drum up some much-needed cash flow. I’ve flagged your account for the state’s rural small business hardship grant and can walk you through the application before tomorrow’s deadline. I’m also willing to table your loan renewal paperwork for two weeks to give you some breathing room.
[He set a stack of neatly printed grant forms on the scuffed concession counter, his usual firm posture relaxing slightly.]

turns.name: Clay Thornton
turns.text:
Back then, we’d have kids sneaking in with paper bags of stolen corn from the rows right over there, and we’d let ’em slide ’cause half of ’em couldn’t afford a ticket anyway. We ran two double features most weekends, and the concession stand ran out of buttered popcorn before the first movie even finished. You folks can’t just let this place get gobbled up by that developer’s cash grab.
[He leans his calloused, grease-stained forearms on the projection booth’s cracked windowsill, rapping a knuckle against the scuffed metal frame of the booth’s outdoor speaker box.]

The bindery’s back shelves are stacked with leather-bound classics and half-finished custom journals, and the air smells like waxed thread and old paper; the library’s director has just notified the family the town council will cut their shared rental space in three months to make way for a free public wifi hub.

characters.tendencies: He has run the Hawthorne Bindery for 45 years, refusing to adopt modern binding equipment because he believes hand-tooled craft is the only way to honor the vintage books the library houses.

characters.tendencies: He is a 17-year-old high school poet and book club president who orders custom journals from the Hawthorne Bindery for his club’s annual chapbook, and he organized a 220-signature petition to keep the bindery open for local creators.

turns.name: Elias Hawthorne
turns.text:
This tattered 1902 edition of Cape Cod Folklore came in with a botched modern glue binding that’s already begun to crumble away the paper’s delicate edge. I’d rather spend three days hand-stitching its custom calfskin cover than slap a quick, disposable binding on it that won’t outlast the summer.
[He sets down his scuffed wooden workbox, weighted with brass hand tools and spools of waxed linen thread, on a weathered wooden crate outside the library’s back alley entrance]

turns.name: Lila Hawthorne
turns.text:
I’ve been tinkering with a new hybrid bindery model that pairs hand-stamped leather covers with editable digital template inserts for custom journals or poetry books. I’m testing a small pop-up right in this alley if the library lets me, and I wanted to hand out free sample sets to anyone passing through.
[She adjusts the frayed canvas bindery apron stained with leather dye, then propped a wobbly collapsible display table against the library’s red brick facade, arranging hand-bound mini notebooks alongside bright QR code flyers linked to her digital template shop.]

turns.name: Marisol "Marcy" Hale
turns.text:
I’ve spent twelve years tending Portside’s collection with only a rickety folding table in the basement’s damp, drafty corner for binding repairs. The council’s proposed wifi hub expansion could spare a tiny sliver of its budget for a proper dedicated bindery space, where we can preserve all the town’s faded fishing logs, old harbor maps, and local newsletter archives instead of letting them rot away.
[She pulls a crumpled hand-drawn sketch of a compact, waterproofed bindery layout from the breast pocket of her tweed blazer and taps the outline with a calloused, ink-stained finger.]

turns.name: Tom Mendez
turns.text:
I brought the final polished poems from the Portside High Book Club’s annual chapbook—we spent all last week passing out petitions around the library and waterfront, and we turned in over 220 signatures to save your shop last week. I just hope we can get our copies printed before our end-of-semester book fair.
[Kneeling to slide the manila folder of stapled-together poem pages under the bindery’s slightly ajar service door, brushing a salt-crusted strand of brown hair off his forehead before giving a shy wave through the smudged front window.]

turns.name: Elias Hawthorne
turns.text:
That hybrid journal scheme’s a fine novelty for souvenir shops, but this 1902 Cape Cod Folklore doesn’t need digital templates or that cheap modern glue ruining its spine. It deserves the same careful hand-sewing and beeswax binding that’s kept books alive along this coast for generations.
[Brushing flecks of dried beeswax from his oil-stained canvas apron before carefully tucking the tattered folio under one arm and grabbing his scuffed bindery hammer from the nearby stack of crates.]

turns.name: Lila Hawthorne
turns.text:
Grandpa, Marcy, Tom—this hybrid bindery model is exactly what we need to keep both our family shop afloat and help Portside finally get proper repair space. We could even print custom digital templates for chapbooks like the ones your book club put together, host small binding workshops in the library’s unused back corner, and use that income to cover our own shop’s upcoming rent shortfall while fixing up fragile library collections like this tattered 1902 folklore book.
[I set down the crumpled stack of lighthouse and seascape-themed digital template prints I’d tucked under my arm, then hold up a hand-stamped leather scrap I’d prepped earlier to show off the hand-binding core of the plan.]

turns.name: Marisol "Marcy" Hale
turns.text:
I’ve spent twelve years making do with that rickety, damp basement folding table for all our binding repairs, and seeing the care everyone’s poured into these projects—from Elias’s rescued 1902 folklore to Lila’s hybrid bindery plans and Tom’s gorgeous chapbook—makes it crystal clear we need that dedicated bindery space. These are exactly the kinds of hands-on, community-focused endeavors that’ll help us preserve our local history and bring more neighbors through our library doors.
[Picks up Lila’s hand-stamped leather journal prototype, running a thumb over the embossed coastal lily design before setting it back carefully against the stack of Tom’s chapbooks.]

turns.name: Tom Mendez
turns.text:
These are the final polished poems for our Portside High Book Club’s annual chapbook, ready for your signature sewn binding just like we agreed. I also wanted to tell you we’ve crossed 230 signatures on the petition to keep your bindery open—way more than I thought we’d hit so fast.
[I set the crisp, staple-free stack of printed poetry on the bindery’s scuffed workbench and rest my thumb on the hand-stamped book club logo on the top page]

scenario.title: Reiger Fly & Tackle’s Crossroads
scenario.setting: Nestled between a salt-crusted clam shack and a driftwood art gallery in coastal La Push, Washington, Reiger Fly & Tackle has operated as a three-generation family shop since 1947. Its weathered clapboard siding is streaked with sea spray and faint rust from decades of displayed casting reels, and the front window balances hand-tied steelhead flies beside dented saltwater tackle passed down from the shop’s original owner. The current owner, Marnie Reiger, received an unexpected 40% rent hike last week, forcing her to choose between leaning into the sustainable fly-tying supplies that draw younger eco-conscious anglers or doubling down on the classic saltwater gear that has kept loyal regulars coming for decades.

turns.name: Marnie Reiger
turns.text:
This shop’s been perched on this La Push boardwalk for 75 years, longer than the neighboring salt-crusted clam shack even started serving their famous buttery chowder. I can’t just swap out my great-grandpa’s hand-tied salmon flies and vintage cedar tackle chests for mass-produced, cheap imported gear just to cover this sudden steep rent hike.
[She brushes salt spray off a shelf of hand-carved driftwood lures she’d been testing as a new inventory item before hunching slightly, crumpling the taped-to-the-door rent notice a little more in her calloused fingers.]

turns.name: Ernie Reiger
turns.text:
I don’t stock any of that trendy fad stuff—this shop’s for serious saltwater anglers, not weekend hobbyists chasing viral fishing hacks. A properly tied bucktail jig or spun deer hair dry fly is all you need to hook a chinook or red rockfish, no flimsy plastic nonsense required.
[Slams a dented metal tin of hand-tied classic salmon flies onto the scuffed Formica counter, glowering at the customer who’d laid out a pack of neon micro-synthetic flies on the register.]

turns.name: Lila Marquez
turns.text:
I’ve had three twenty-something and teen anglers ask about sustainable fly-tying materials already this shift. Swapping our stock of cheap synthetic furs for foraged local feathers and naturally shed deer mane would draw in that eco-conscious crowd and boost our bottom line without alienating our regulars.
[I lean across the scuffed, salt-stained wooden counter and tap a glass jar brimming with iridescent, locally harvested abalone shell scraps, which make brilliant, zero-waste bead eyes for hand-tied flies.]

turns.name: Jake Torres
turns.text:
Hey, how’s it goin’? I heard you guys revamped your inventory recently, and I was worried I’d lose access to the Shimano big-game reels I’ve used for my commercial cod runs for years. Also, my teen boy’s been begging for premium wool bug bodies for his fly-tying projects, so I wanted to pick those up too.
[He sets a salt-crusted commercial fishing glove on the scuffed wooden counter, shoving a crumpled, fish-stained note scrawled with his requested items out toward the clerk.]

turns.name: Marnie Reiger
turns.text:
Jake, thank goodness you stopped by—we’re not getting rid of your go-to Shimano big-game reels, not on your or Dad’s watch. We’re just adding a small curated section of sustainable fly-tying supplies to keep up with steady customer demand and cover the sudden rent hike that landed in our mailbox last week.
[Reaches under the scuffed pine counter and pulls out a dented cardboard box stenciled "eco supplies" in fading white paint, its edges crusted with coastal salt from the boardwalk’s sea spray]

turns.name: Ernie Reiger
turns.text:
Sustainable fly materials? That’s a marketing gimmick, not serious tackle. I’ve relied on deer hair and bucktail for 40 years, and this shop won’t stock anything that undercuts the classic gear that’s kept saltwater anglers landing trophy fish for generations. You won’t lose your go-to Shimano big-game reels here—we’re not ditching the reliable stuff for flash-in-the-pan trends.
[He nods toward the wall lined with polished vintage big-game reels, then taps a jar of hand-tied natural bucktail flies bolted to the countertop.]

turns.name: Lila Marquez
turns.text:
"Three of those younger, eco-conscious anglers already asked about sustainable fly-tying supplies this shift, folks who care about protecting the coastal waters we love to fish. Shifting just a portion of our stock to ethically sourced, eco-friendly materials would bring in this loyal, growing customer base without alienating our regular serious saltwater crew."
[I gesture to the clear tackle tray I set on the shop’s counter, filled with hand-tied flies made from recycled sinew and naturally shed local deer hair.]

turns.text:
Hey, how’s it goin’? I heard you guys revamped your inventory recently, and I was worried I’d lose access to the Shimano big-game reels I’ve used for salmon charters out of Neah Bay for the last decade. Figured I’d swing by to confirm you still carry the heavy-duty models I rely on, though my teen son’s been pestering me to pick up some sustainable fly-tying supplies for his own small freshwater projects lately.

Its former concession stand now sells craft cider and vegan pretzels instead of buttered popcorn, its projection booth repurposed as a soundboard station, and a small group of lifelong residents is fighting to restore its vintage art deco marquee and host monthly classic film screenings alongside the indie folk and punk shows booked by the venue’s young manager.

turns.name: Marv Pritchard
turns.text:
I’ve been showing up to this theater for classic matinees since I was 10, and I can’t believe the city’s even considering funding permanent live performance upgrades that’d gut the kind of quiet, communal film nights we’ve been running out of the side lounge for two years now. This spot’s legacy isn’t stage lights—it’s big screen blockbusters and Saturday cartoons.
[He adjusts the stack of 16mm film canisters tucked under his arm and smooths a crumpled screening flyer taped crookedly to the concession stand’s side.]

turns.name: Lila Torres
turns.text:
I just confirmed that local indie shoegaze act Soft Signal will play our first VIP balcony showcase next Friday, once we finish patching the drywall in the upper seating area. We already have 42 pre-sold tickets for the spot, which is double what we thought we’d hit in just three days of spreading the word.
[kneeling to brush a layer of dust off the weathered brass plaque marking the theater’s original 1972 balcony entrance, tucked behind the concession stand’s stack of unopened popcorn bags]

turns.name: Javi Ruiz
turns.text:
Good evening, everyone packed into this beloved chipped red-brick Orion Theater—whether you’re a lifelong regular or here for your first hybrid film-music night! We’re kicking things off with a rare 1972 Saturday matinee cartoon clip before the local folk quartet takes the live stage.
[I adjust the height of the projection screen hanging above the stage, running a hand to smooth out a tiny crease in the fabric.]

turns.name: Gloria Wade
turns.text:
Good evening, neighbors popping by the Orion tonight! This month’s community newsletter drops right now, with full listings for our upcoming 1970s retro double features and a roundup of local acts playing the theater’s lobby shows all summer. It’s such a joy to see this old beloved brick spot filled with folks who want to keep its warm spirit alive.
[Brushing a fleck of chipped red brick dust off a stack of freshly printed newsletters before tucking a handful under the concession stand’s front ledge for passersby to grab]

turns.name: Marv Pritchard
turns.text:
Hold up, let’s get our priorities straight first. We’re here to sort out booking the side lounge for next month’s Saturday matinee of *Paper Moon*, not vote on permanent live performance setups that’ll jack up our monthly overhead for years to come. This theater’s legacy is tied to classic Hollywood films, not random indie band showcases.
[Grabs a tattered stack of classic film reservation slips from his canvas bag and slaps them down sharply on the chipped concession counter.]

turns.text:
Good evening, everyone—thanks to the newsletter Gloria just shared, we have official sign-up sheets out by the box office for our first balcony VIP showcase next Friday with Soft Signal. For anyone who’s loved this theater through decades of movies and matinees, this is our chance to save that empty upper level and turn it into a space for intimate live music.
[I lean up to tap the weathered wooden railing of the half-restored balcony overhead, then hold up a stack of bright magenta event flyers to wave at the front rows of the crowd.]

Whether you’re a lifelong regular or here for your first hybrid film-music night, thank you all for packing into this chipped Orion tonight. Drop a suggestion for your favorite classic film to screen next month in the box by the front door too!

scenario.title: Elara’s Orchard: Blight and Branching Choices
scenario.setting: Elara’s Orchard is divided into 12 interconnected microcells: heirloom apple guild beds, mason bee nesting boxes, rain-harvest cisterns, and stone fruit barrier rows. Planted by their great-grandmother 13 years prior, it’s now sustained by three sibling stewards and a rotating crew of local volunteers, having cleared its first critical growth year and entered its second decade of production. The core dilemma hinges on the orchard’s original cider apple tree, whose root flare shows signs of neonatal blight, splitting the siblings over how best to save it.

characters.name: Mara
characters.tendencies: She curates the siblings' shared digital archive of great-grandma's orchard notes, cross-referencing weekly microcell surveys against Elara’s original planting plan. She refuses to consider untested treatments because she fears losing the orchard's original ancestral lineage.

characters.name: Lila
characters.tendencies: She’s spent the last three months trialing organic copper sulfate sprays on the affected tree, refining application rates to minimize harm to nearby pollinator habitats. She argues that delaying the experimental treatment will lead to the tree's death before the autumn harvest.

characters.name: Javi
characters.tendencies: He runs the orchard’s community-supported agriculture program, hosting monthly open houses and recruiting local volunteers to assist with daily maintenance. He worries that diverting all their resources to saving one tree will leave other parts of the orchard’s microcell network under-cared for.

characters.name: Kaelin
characters.tendencies: They’re a local teen volunteer who first discovered the orchard through Javi’s social media posts, and they’ve begun documenting the orchard’s unplanned volunteer saplings. They’ve noticed new shoots sprouting from the base of the blighted tree, and they advocate for letting natural regeneration lead the way.
